title: Beyond the Highest Salary: Choosing a Quantitative Career
text: As a graduate student in Applied Economics and Data Science with a Financial Mathematics background, I face a practical question: which careers deserve my limited job-search and preparation time? The highest salary is tempting, but it says little about the size of a job market or the preparation a role requires. I compare four relevant paths: data science, operations research, financial and investment analysis, and actuarial work.

title: Beyond the Highest Salary: Choosing a Quantitative Career
text:
Collecting comparable evidence
I scraped four public O*NET® OnLine occupation profiles using R’s rvest package. These pages report BLS wage and employment data in a consistent format. This is a purposeful comparison of four careers, not a representative sample of all graduate jobs.
The script below identifies HTML field labels, extracts their adjacent values, removes dollar signs and commas, and saves numeric columns. It checks occupation names and reference periods before producing a CSV. Financial and investment analysts is a specific occupational category; I do not combine its salary with the broader financial-analyst category’s openings.


Show the complete rvest collection and cleaning script

# Collect and clean four O*NET occupation profiles.
# Run from the post2 directory. Existing snapshots are reused by default.

career_sources <- data.frame(
  soc = c("15-2051.00", "15-2031.00", "13-2051.00", "15-2011.00"),
  occupation = c("Data Scientists", "Operations Research Analysts",
                 "Financial and Investment Analysts", "Actuaries"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
career_sources$url <- paste0("https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/",
                             career_sources$soc)
research_agent <- paste0("StudentCareerResearch/1.0 (contact: ",
                        "https://qianzhaoli949-afk.github.io/qianzhao-website/)")

# Pause between requests and stop on HTTP errors.
fetch_html <- function(url, dest) {
  Sys.sleep(4)
  page <- rvest::session(url, httr::user_agent(research_agent), httr::timeout(30))
  status <- httr::status_code(page$response)
  if (status != 200L) stop("Fetch stopped: HTTP ", status, " at ", url)
  writeBin(page$response$content, dest)
  invisible(format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE))
}

# Extract the value following a matching field label.
field <- function(doc, prefix) {
  labels <- rvest::html_elements(doc, "#WagesEmployment dt")
  text <- rvest::html_text2(labels)
  hit <- which(startsWith(text, prefix))
  if (length(hit) != 1L) stop("Expected one field: ", prefix)
  value <- rvest::html_element(labels[[hit]], xpath = "following-sibling::dd[1]")
  list(label = text[hit], value = rvest::html_text2(value))
}

match_one <- function(text, pattern) {
  hit <- regmatches(text, regexec(pattern, text, perl = TRUE))[[1]]
  if (length(hit) < 2L) stop("Could not parse: ", text)
  hit[2]
}

parse_career <- function(path, soc, url, retrieved_utc) {
  doc <- rvest::read_html(path)
  title <- rvest::html_text2(rvest::html_element(doc, "h1 .main"))
  pay <- field(doc, "Median wages")
  employment <- field(doc, "Employment (")
  growth <- field(doc, "Projected growth")
  openings <- field(doc, "Projected job openings")
  education <- rvest::html_text2(rvest::html_elements(doc, "#Education li"))
  # Keep NA when the education section is absent.
  degree <- NA_character_
  share <- NA_real_
  if (length(education)) {
    shares <- as.numeric(vapply(education, match_one, character(1),
                               pattern = "^([0-9]+)%"))
    top <- which.max(shares)
    degree <- trimws(sub("^[0-9]+%\\s*(responded:\\s*)?", "",
                        education[top], perl = TRUE))
    share <- shares[top]
  }
  period <- function(x) match_one(x, "\\(([0-9]{4}[-\u2013][0-9]{4})\\)")
  wage <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", match_one(pay$value, "\\$([0-9,]+) annual")))
  jobs <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", openings$value))
  if (!is.finite(wage) || !is.finite(jobs) || wage <= 0 || jobs <= 0)
    stop("Invalid wage/openings for ", soc)
  if (period(growth$label) != period(openings$label))
    stop("Mismatched projection periods for ", soc)
  data.frame(
    soc = soc, occupation = title, median_annual_pay_usd = wage,
    wage_year = as.integer(match_one(pay$label, "([0-9]{4})")),
    employment = as.numeric(gsub(",", "", match_one(employment$value, "^([0-9,]+)"))),
    employment_year = as.integer(match_one(employment$label, "([0-9]{4})")),
    growth_category = growth$value, projection_period = period(growth$label),
    annual_projected_openings = jobs,
    top_education_response = degree, education_response_pct = share,
    education_all_responses = if (length(education)) paste(education, collapse = " | ") else NA_character_,
    source_url = url, retrieved_utc = retrieved_utc,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

build_careers <- function(data_dir = "data", refresh = FALSE) {
  if (!requireNamespace("rvest", quietly = TRUE) ||
      !requireNamespace("httr", quietly = TRUE))
    stop('Install packages first: install.packages(c("rvest", "httr"))')
  raw_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "raw")
  dir.create(raw_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  manifest_file <- file.path(data_dir, "manifest.csv")
  manifest <- if (file.exists(manifest_file)) {
    read.csv(manifest_file, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  } else {
    data.frame(soc = character(), url = character(), retrieved_utc = character(),
               file = character(), md5 = character())
  }
  paths <- file.path(raw_dir, paste0(career_sources$soc, ".html"))
  needs_fetch <- refresh | !file.exists(paths)
  if (any(needs_fetch)) {
    robots_file <- file.path(data_dir, "robots.txt")
    fetch_html("https://www.onetonline.org/robots.txt", robots_file)
    rules <- readLines(robots_file, warn = FALSE)
    # Require a new policy review if robots.txt has changed.
    if (!file.exists("ROBOTS-REVIEWED.txt") ||
        !identical(rules, readLines("ROBOTS-REVIEWED.txt", warn = FALSE)))
      stop("robots.txt needs manual review before collecting; see DATA-NOTES.md.")
    for (i in which(needs_fetch)) {
      stamp <- fetch_html(career_sources$url[i], paths[i])
      manifest <- manifest[manifest$soc != career_sources$soc[i], , drop = FALSE]
      manifest <- rbind(manifest, data.frame(
        soc = career_sources$soc[i], url = career_sources$url[i],
        retrieved_utc = stamp, file = basename(paths[i]),
        md5 = unname(tools::md5sum(paths[i]))
      ))
      write.csv(manifest, manifest_file, row.names = FALSE)
    }
  }
  rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(career_sources)), function(i) {
    m <- manifest[manifest$soc == career_sources$soc[i], , drop = FALSE]
    if (nrow(m) != 1L || m$md5 != unname(tools::md5sum(paths[i])))
      stop("Missing or changed snapshot for ", career_sources$soc[i])
    parse_career(paths[i], career_sources$soc[i], career_sources$url[i], m$retrieved_utc)
  })
  result <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  if (!identical(result$occupation, career_sources$occupation))
    stop("Occupation labels have changed; review the source pages.")
  if (length(unique(result$wage_year)) != 1L ||
      length(unique(result$projection_period)) != 1L)
    stop("Sources mix reference years; review before comparing.")
  write.csv(result, file.path(data_dir, "careers.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
  result
}

I checked the site’s robots rules and content license, used an identifiable user agent, and spaced requests four seconds apart. The script stops on HTTP errors and saves dated HTML snapshots. Re-rendering uses these snapshots, so it adds no traffic. No login, CAPTCHA, or access restriction was bypassed.
The snapshot was collected on September 19, 2026, in New York (September 20 UTC). It contains 2025 wages and 2024–2034 employment projections, as published by O*NET at collection time. These are different reference periods and should not be described as a single year’s observations. Growth is published in categories, so I preserve those labels rather than inventing precise percentages.

title: Beyond the Highest Salary: Choosing a Quantitative Career
section: Pay and opportunity tell different stories
text:
Pay and opportunity tell different stories








Figure 1: National occupational median pay (2025) versus projected average annual openings (2024–2034). Source: BLS data displayed by O*NET OnLine; saved September 19, 2026 (New York).





Actuaries have the highest median pay, $130,000, but only 2,400 projected annual openings. Data scientists combine $120,230 median pay with 23,400 openings—about 9.8 times the actuarial total. For someone still exploring career directions, that difference makes data science worth investigating alongside the salary leader.
Financial and investment analysts have the most openings in this comparison, 25,100, despite a lower median wage of $102,740. Operations research offers 9,600 openings and $88,940 median pay. Its emphasis on quantitative decision-making makes it relevant to my training even though its wage is lower.
Preparation also matters. In the available O*NET education responses, 48% of data-science respondents identify a bachelor’s degree as required, while 43% of operations-research respondents identify a master’s degree. These are survey responses, not universal hiring rules. The financial-and-investment profile lacks this education breakdown; the script records it as missing rather than guessing.

title: Beyond the Highest Salary: Choosing a Quantitative Career
section: Turning the comparison into a decision
text:
Turning the comparison into a decision
I would start by exploring data-science and financial-and-investment analyst roles. Data science combines strong pay, fast projected growth, and many openings relative to its size. Financial analysis offers the largest number of openings. The growth comparison also gives me a reason to take operations research more seriously, rather than dismissing it because of its lower pay.
Next, I would review ten entry-level vacancies in each of the first two careers, list the skills employers ask for most often, and build a relevant project for each. I would keep operations research on my shortlist too. The data help me narrow my search, but my interests and preparation still matter.
Actuarial work remains attractive if I want its specialized preparation: BLS describes a series of professional exams. I would investigate that commitment before choosing it solely for higher pay.
The comparison has limits. Median pay does not tell me what a new graduate earns. Projected annual openings include growth and replacement needs, not just entry-level jobs or current vacancies. More openings do not necessarily mean an easier job search because I do not know how many people will apply. The national figures also leave out local living costs and work-authorization requirements. I would use all three measures—pay, growth, and openings—to guide my search, then check actual job ads.

title: Why More Income Can Mean Less Instant Noodles
text:
It sounds backwards: why would a person buy less of something after getting a raise? In economics, a product with that pattern is called an inferior good. The word “inferior” is easy to misunderstand. It does not mean the product is unsafe, low quality, or morally worse. It simply describes how a consumer’s demand changes when income changes, holding prices and preferences constant.
An inferior good has a negative income elasticity of demand:
\[
\text{Income elasticity of demand} =
\frac{\%\text{ change in quantity demanded}}{\%\text{ change in income}} < 0.
\]
In plain language, when income rises, the quantity demanded falls. When income falls, the quantity demanded rises. This result is unintuitive because we often expect people to buy more of everything when they can afford more. But people do not only buy more; they also change what they buy.

title: Why More Income Can Mean Less Instant Noodles
text:
A practical example
Imagine a student who regularly buys instant noodles because they are cheap, quick, and easy to store. When the student’s budget expands, they may replace some noodle meals with fresh ingredients, restaurant meals, or other convenient options they prefer. Instant noodles have not changed. The student’s choices have changed because better alternatives are now within reach.
The figure below uses a small, hypothetical example. It shows monthly instant noodle purchases for households at different monthly incomes. The downward line illustrates the defining pattern of an inferior good: higher income is associated with fewer noodle packages purchased. The numbers are invented for teaching purposes, so this figure demonstrates the concept rather than making a claim about a real population.

# Hypothetical data created for this example; no external data source is used.
income <- c(1500, 2500, 3500, 4500, 5500, 6500)
noodle_packages <- c(18, 15, 12, 9, 7, 5)

plot(
  income, noodle_packages,
  type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#2C7FB8", lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Monthly household income (USD)",
  ylab = "Instant noodle packages purchased per month",
  main = "An illustrative inferior good",
  ylim = c(0, 20)
)
grid(col = "gray85")







Figure 1: Illustrative demand for an inferior good: instant noodles.





This graph should not be read as proof that instant noodles are inferior for every household. A good can be inferior for one person, at one income level, and not for another. For example, someone who likes instant noodles as a snack may buy more of them after a raise. Economists therefore estimate income elasticities from data instead of assigning a permanent label to every product.
It is also helpful to separate inferior goods from Giffen goods. A Giffen good is a rare special case in which a price increase leads consumers to buy more of the good. Inferior goods concern changes in income, while Giffen goods concern changes in price. Some Giffen goods must be inferior, but most inferior goods are not Giffen goods. Treating the two as identical is one of the most common mistakes in introductory economics.

title: Why More Income Can Mean Less Instant Noodles
text:
Takeaway
“Inferior” is a technical description of consumer behavior, not a judgment of a product. When income rises, consumers may move away from budget-oriented choices toward alternatives they value more. The concept is a useful reminder that higher income changes the composition of spending, not just its total.

title: Why More Income Can Mean Less Instant Noodles

Data source and reproducibility
This post uses no external data. The six observations in the R code are hypothetical values created solely to visualize the definition of an inferior good. Running the code block reproduces the figure.

title: Education and Work: What Unemployment Rates Leave Out
text: When unemployment falls, does that mean more people have jobs? Not necessarily: the unemployment rate excludes adults who are not looking for work. This matters when we compare education groups after a major labor-market shock. I use the Current Population Survey (CPS) to ask how unemployment changed from 2019 to 2024, whether employment among all adults followed the same path, and whether the education pattern also appears within age groups.

title: Education and Unemployment: How Did the Gap Change?
text:
Measuring unemployment consistently
The extract contains all 72 Basic Monthly samples from January 2019 to December 2024, restricted to ages 25–64. This focuses on working-age adults beyond the usual college years. I group education into less than high school, high school, some college or an associate degree, and a bachelor’s degree or higher. These groups describe completed education, not current enrollment.
Every estimate uses WTFINL, the monthly person weight. The unemployment rate is weighted unemployed people divided by the weighted civilian labor force, not all adults:
\[
u_g = 100\frac{\sum_{i\in g} w_i\,1(\text{unemployed}_i)}
{\sum_{i\in g} w_i\,1(\text{employed or unemployed}_i)}.
\]
People outside the labor force do not enter this denominator. Annual rates divide the sum of monthly weighted unemployment totals by the sum of monthly weighted labor-force totals. They are ratios of annual-average levels, not simple averages of monthly percentages. All figures are not seasonally adjusted.

title: Education and Unemployment: Unequal Shocks, Uneven Recovery
section: 1. The shock amplified an existing gap
text:
1. The shock amplified an existing gap



Monthly unemployment rates by education. The shaded interval marks March–June 2020.


The monthly view reveals the abrupt disruption that annual averages can hide. All four groups experienced a sharp increase in spring 2020, followed by a decline. The spike was much larger for adults without a high school diploma than for college graduates. Education differences were visible before the pandemic and persisted afterward. The lines therefore suggest unequal exposure to a shared shock, rather than two entirely separate labor markets.

title: Education and Unemployment: Unequal Shocks, Uneven Recovery
section: 2. Recovery did not quite restore the baseline
text:
2. Recovery did not quite restore the baseline



Annual unemployment rates for 2019, 2020, and 2024, calculated from weighted monthly totals.


Among adults without a high school diploma, unemployment rose from 5.5% in 2019 to 11.7% in 2020. For adults with a bachelor’s degree or higher, it rose from 2.1% to 4.7%. The difference between these groups widened from 3.4 to 7.0 percentage points.
By 2024, their rates had fallen to 6.3% and 2.3%, respectively. Each group’s 2024 estimate remained above its 2019 value. This is a descriptive comparison, not a claim that these small remaining differences are statistically significant.

title: Education and Unemployment: Unequal Shocks, Uneven Recovery
section: 3. Age composition is not the whole story
text:
3. Age composition is not the whole story



Annual rates within three age groups. Points show only 2019, 2020, and 2024; connecting segments are visual guides. All panels use the same vertical scale and WTFINL weights.


Education groups may contain different mixes of younger and older workers. Splitting the sample into ages 25–34, 35–49, and 50–64 checks whether that mix alone explains the pattern. The broad education gradient appears within each age band, including during the pandemic. However, these are still broad groups: occupation, industry, experience, and other characteristics may differ within them. This is not an age-adjusted causal estimate of a degree’s value.

title: Education and Unemployment: How Did the Gap Change?
text:
Takeaway and limitations
The figures tell a specific story. All four groups had higher unemployment in 2020 than in 2019. The percentage-point gap between the lowest and highest education groups grew in 2020 and narrowed by 2024, while the rate ratio tells a different story about 2019–2020. The age panels also show differences within broad age groups. These findings describe who had higher unemployment and how the rates changed; they do not explain why or tell us which policy would help.
CPS respondents can appear in multiple months, so the 3,835,958 retained records are person-month observations, not unique people. The charts present weighted point estimates without confidence intervals. Pandemic-era collection disruptions and lower response rates also warrant caution. Finally, unemployment alone cannot reveal whether people left the labor force, accepted fewer hours, or experienced wage losses.

title: Education and Work: What Unemployment Rates Leave Out
text:
Data and reproducibility
Source: IPUMS CPS, University of Minnesota, using underlying U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics data. I use all 72 Basic Monthly samples from January 2019 through December 2024 and group completed education into four levels. The unemployment denominator includes employed and unemployed adults who are looking for work; the employment-share denominator includes all civilians in each group. Annual rates use sums of weighted monthly counts, not simple averages of monthly percentages. The extract was created September 27, 2026. Education definitions follow IPUMS EDUC documentation.
Download the code and grouped summaries, analysis script, plotting script, annual gap calculations, and reproduction instructions. The GitHub repository contains this post under blog/posts/post3/. title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
text: What changed a new-home buyer’s monthly payment more between late 2019 and late 2024: the home’s price or the mortgage rate? In my model, the payment rose about $671 per month in 2024 dollars. Changing only the rate adds about $580; changing only the inflation-adjusted price adds about $66. The two changes also interact, adding the remaining $26. The rate increase did most of the work.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
section: From three series to a comparable payment
text:
From three series to a comparable payment
I download three series programmatically from FRED: Census/HUD’s median new-home sales price (MSPUS), Freddie Mac’s 30-year mortgage rate (MORTGAGE30US), and BLS’s all-items CPI (CPIAUCNS). These are new data for this blog, distinct from the earlier O*NET and CPS projects.
The price series is quarterly. I average weekly mortgage observations and the three monthly CPI observations within each quarter, producing 40 quarters from 2015 through 2024. I stop at 2024 because the downloaded CPI series has no October 2025 observation; I do not impute it or average an incomplete quarter. All three series are not seasonally adjusted. Endpoint comparisons use Q4 in both years, although that does not remove all seasonal influences.
For a hypothetical purchase each quarter, I assume a 20% down payment and a fully amortizing 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Monthly principal and interest are
\[
M=0.8P\frac{r/1200}{1-(1+r/1200)^{-360}},
\]
where \(P\) is the sales price and \(r\) is the annual interest rate in percent. Multiplying prices and payments by \(CPI_{2024Q4}/CPI_t\) expresses them in 2024 Q4 dollars. These transformations make monetary comparisons meaningful without confusing general inflation with housing-specific changes.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
section: 1. The price and the financing cost are different moving parts
text:
1. The price and the financing cost are different moving parts



Real median new-home prices and quarterly-average mortgage rates. Sources: Census/HUD, Freddie Mac, and BLS via FRED.


The first figure separates the two inputs rather than putting unlike units on a dual axis. From 2019 Q4 to 2024 Q4, the real median price changed by 4.5%, while the average mortgage rate moved from 3.7% to 6.6%. Price movements alone therefore cannot describe the change faced by a financed buyer.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
section: 2. Translate those inputs into monthly dollars
text:
2. Translate those inputs into monthly dollars



Illustrative real monthly payments, with a comparison holding the rate at its 2019 Q4 level. Calculations use 20% down and a 30-year term.


The modeled real payment rose from $1,478 to $2,149, a 45.4% increase. The dashed line keeps each quarter’s price but holds the interest rate fixed at its 2019 Q4 value. By 2024 Q4, that calculation yields $1,544, or $606 less per month than the contemporaneous-rate scenario. This is a controlled arithmetic comparison, not a claim that buyers could actually obtain the old rate.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
section: 3. Change one input at a time
text:
3. Change one input at a time



Four Q4 endpoint scenarios in constant purchasing-power dollars. The middle bars change only real price or only interest rate.


The third figure holds the other input constant in each middle bar. The price-only change adds $66 to the baseline payment; the rate-only change adds $580. These separate increments need not sum to the combined increase: a higher rate also applies to the changed loan amount. The chart isolates the financing mechanism, rather than estimating a causal effect of monetary policy on prices.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
text:
Takeaway and limits
Evaluating a home by its sticker price alone misses a major part of the financing calculation. A practical budgeting exercise should vary both the price and the offered rate, then add taxes, insurance, maintenance, and fees, which are excluded here. The down payment itself is another constraint.
These are illustrative payments for new buyers, not average payments of existing homeowners. New-home medians change with the mix of homes sold and are not a constant-quality price index. National series mask local differences; the mortgage benchmark is not an individual loan quote. Freddie Mac also changed its survey methodology in November 2022. Without household income, credit, or wealth data, the figures cannot tell us who can afford to buy.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
text:
Reproduce the analysis
The README documents folders, assumptions, and commands. Analysis code, plotting code, quarterly data, income comparison, and download provenance are available alongside the GitHub repository. Ordinary rendering checks and reuses saved downloads; an explicit refresh retrieves new data, which may include revisions.

title: Beyond the Highest Salary: Choosing a Quantitative Career
section: Growth, market size, and openings are different signals
text:
Growth, market size, and openings are different signals
The growth labels add information that salary and openings alone miss. Data scientists, operations research analysts, and actuaries all fall in the 7% or higher projected employment-growth category for 2024–2034. Financial and investment analysts fall in 5% to 6%. These are cumulative ten-year net growth categories, not annual growth rates. The open-ended category does not tell us which of the first three occupations grows fastest, so assigning all three an exact 7% value would create false precision.








Figure 2: Color shows projected net employment-growth categories; bar length shows gross annual openings relative to 2024 employment. Source: saved O*NET profiles, BLS projections for 2024–2034.





To separate opportunity volume from occupational size, I calculate 100 × projected average annual openings / 2024 employment. Unlike net growth, openings also include replacement needs. This ratio is a scale-adjusted comparison, not an annual growth rate, vacancy rate, or probability of getting hired.

Actuarial work has fast projected net growth but the fewest absolute openings because its base market is small. Thus, a fast-growing occupation need not offer the largest number of opportunities; market size and growth answer different questions.

title: Beyond the Highest Salary: Choosing a Quantitative Career
text:
Collecting and cleaning the data
I scraped four public O*NET® OnLine occupation profiles using R’s rvest package. These pages report BLS wage and employment data in a consistent format. I chose these careers because they relate to my studies, so the comparison does not cover every option for graduates.
My script finds the relevant labels on each page and extracts the values beside them. It removes dollar signs and commas so R can read the numbers, then checks the occupation names and years. I use the same occupation category for wages and openings rather than mixing different types of financial analysts.


Show the complete rvest collection and cleaning script

# Collect and clean four O*NET occupation profiles.
# Run from the post2 directory. Existing snapshots are reused by default.

career_sources <- data.frame(
  soc = c("15-2051.00", "15-2031.00", "13-2051.00", "15-2011.00"),
  occupation = c("Data Scientists", "Operations Research Analysts",
                 "Financial and Investment Analysts", "Actuaries"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
career_sources$url <- paste0("https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/",
                             career_sources$soc)
research_agent <- paste0("StudentCareerResearch/1.0 (contact: ",
                        "https://qianzhaoli949-afk.github.io/qianzhao-website/)")

# Pause between requests and stop on HTTP errors.
fetch_html <- function(url, dest) {
  Sys.sleep(4)
  page <- rvest::session(url, httr::user_agent(research_agent), httr::timeout(30))
  status <- httr::status_code(page$response)
  if (status != 200L) stop("Fetch stopped: HTTP ", status, " at ", url)
  writeBin(page$response$content, dest)
  invisible(format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE))
}

# Extract the value following a matching field label.
field <- function(doc, prefix) {
  labels <- rvest::html_elements(doc, "#WagesEmployment dt")
  text <- rvest::html_text2(labels)
  hit <- which(startsWith(text, prefix))
  if (length(hit) != 1L) stop("Expected one field: ", prefix)
  value <- rvest::html_element(labels[[hit]], xpath = "following-sibling::dd[1]")
  list(label = text[hit], value = rvest::html_text2(value))
}

match_one <- function(text, pattern) {
  hit <- regmatches(text, regexec(pattern, text, perl = TRUE))[[1]]
  if (length(hit) < 2L) stop("Could not parse: ", text)
  hit[2]
}

parse_career <- function(path, soc, url, retrieved_utc) {
  doc <- rvest::read_html(path)
  title <- rvest::html_text2(rvest::html_element(doc, "h1 .main"))
  pay <- field(doc, "Median wages")
  employment <- field(doc, "Employment (")
  growth <- field(doc, "Projected growth")
  openings <- field(doc, "Projected job openings")
  education <- rvest::html_text2(rvest::html_elements(doc, "#Education li"))
  # Keep NA when the education section is absent.
  degree <- NA_character_
  share <- NA_real_
  if (length(education)) {
    shares <- as.numeric(vapply(education, match_one, character(1),
                               pattern = "^([0-9]+)%"))
    top <- which.max(shares)
    degree <- trimws(sub("^[0-9]+%\\s*(responded:\\s*)?", "",
                        education[top], perl = TRUE))
    share <- shares[top]
  }
  period <- function(x) match_one(x, "\\(([0-9]{4}[-\u2013][0-9]{4})\\)")
  wage <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", match_one(pay$value, "\\$([0-9,]+) annual")))
  jobs <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", openings$value))
  if (!is.finite(wage) || !is.finite(jobs) || wage <= 0 || jobs <= 0)
    stop("Invalid wage/openings for ", soc)
  if (period(growth$label) != period(openings$label))
    stop("Mismatched projection periods for ", soc)
  data.frame(
    soc = soc, occupation = title, median_annual_pay_usd = wage,
    wage_year = as.integer(match_one(pay$label, "([0-9]{4})")),
    employment = as.numeric(gsub(",", "", match_one(employment$value, "^([0-9,]+)"))),
    employment_year = as.integer(match_one(employment$label, "([0-9]{4})")),
    growth_category = growth$value, projection_period = period(growth$label),
    annual_projected_openings = jobs,
    top_education_response = degree, education_response_pct = share,
    education_all_responses = if (length(education)) paste(education, collapse = " | ") else NA_character_,
    source_url = url, retrieved_utc = retrieved_utc,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

build_careers <- function(data_dir = "data", refresh = FALSE) {
  if (!requireNamespace("rvest", quietly = TRUE) ||
      !requireNamespace("httr", quietly = TRUE))
    stop('Install packages first: install.packages(c("rvest", "httr"))')
  raw_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "raw")
  dir.create(raw_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  manifest_file <- file.path(data_dir, "manifest.csv")
  manifest <- if (file.exists(manifest_file)) {
    read.csv(manifest_file, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  } else {
    data.frame(soc = character(), url = character(), retrieved_utc = character(),
               file = character(), md5 = character())
  }
  paths <- file.path(raw_dir, paste0(career_sources$soc, ".html"))
  needs_fetch <- refresh | !file.exists(paths)
  if (any(needs_fetch)) {
    robots_file <- file.path(data_dir, "robots.txt")
    fetch_html("https://www.onetonline.org/robots.txt", robots_file)
    rules <- readLines(robots_file, warn = FALSE)
    # Require a new policy review if robots.txt has changed.
    if (!file.exists("ROBOTS-REVIEWED.txt") ||
        !identical(rules, readLines("ROBOTS-REVIEWED.txt", warn = FALSE)))
      stop("robots.txt needs manual review before collecting; see DATA-NOTES.md.")
    for (i in which(needs_fetch)) {
      stamp <- fetch_html(career_sources$url[i], paths[i])
      manifest <- manifest[manifest$soc != career_sources$soc[i], , drop = FALSE]
      manifest <- rbind(manifest, data.frame(
        soc = career_sources$soc[i], url = career_sources$url[i],
        retrieved_utc = stamp, file = basename(paths[i]),
        md5 = unname(tools::md5sum(paths[i]))
      ))
      write.csv(manifest, manifest_file, row.names = FALSE)
    }
  }
  rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(career_sources)), function(i) {
    m <- manifest[manifest$soc == career_sources$soc[i], , drop = FALSE]
    if (nrow(m) != 1L || m$md5 != unname(tools::md5sum(paths[i])))
      stop("Missing or changed snapshot for ", career_sources$soc[i])
    parse_career(paths[i], career_sources$soc[i], career_sources$url[i], m$retrieved_utc)
  })
  result <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  if (!identical(result$occupation, career_sources$occupation))
    stop("Occupation labels have changed; review the source pages.")
  if (length(unique(result$wage_year)) != 1L ||
      length(unique(result$projection_period)) != 1L)
    stop("Sources mix reference years; review before comparing.")
  write.csv(result, file.path(data_dir, "careers.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
  result
}

I checked the site’s robots rules and content license, used an identifiable user agent, and spaced requests four seconds apart. The script stops on HTTP errors and saves dated HTML snapshots. Re-rendering uses these snapshots, so it adds no traffic. I did not bypass logins, CAPTCHAs, or access restrictions.
I collected the pages on September 19, 2026, in New York (September 20 UTC). ONET reported 2025 wages and 2024–2034 employment projections. These figures refer to different periods. ONET also reports growth in categories, so I keep those labels instead of treating them as exact percentages.

title: Beyond the Highest Salary: Choosing a Quantitative Career
section: Does faster growth mean more opportunities?
text:
Does faster growth mean more opportunities?
O*NET projects employment growth of 7% or higher for data scientists, operations research analysts, and actuaries over 2024–2034. It places financial and investment analysts in the 5% to 6% group. These categories describe the change in the number of jobs over ten years, not each year. They also do not tell us which of the first three careers will grow fastest: “7% or higher” does not mean exactly 7%.








Figure 2: Color shows projected net employment-growth categories; bar length shows gross annual openings relative to 2024 employment. Source: saved O*NET profiles, BLS projections for 2024–2034.





Larger occupations can have more openings simply because they have more jobs. To account for size, I divide projected annual openings by employment in 2024 and multiply by 100. This gives annual openings per 100 existing jobs. Openings include both new jobs and opportunities to replace workers who leave. The measure does not show annual employment growth, current vacancies, or my chance of getting hired.

title: A Growing State, but Not Everywhere
text:
Living in Philadelphia makes me curious about how the rest of Pennsylvania is changing. Does population growth spread across the state, or does it concentrate in a few places? The answer matters for decisions about housing, transportation, and local services. A growing state can still contain many communities that lose residents.
I use the Census Bureau’s Vintage 2024 county population estimates and its 2024 county boundaries. I keep this fixed release for reproducibility; it is not the newest Census vintage. My comparison runs from the April 1, 2020 estimates base to July 1, 2024. That starting point is the Census Bureau’s population-estimates base, not simply a count from the decennial census.

title: A Growing State, but Not Everywhere
section: A small statewide gain hides a divided map
text:
A small statewide gain hides a divided map
Pennsylvania gained 75,842 residents, or about 0.6%, over this period. Yet 39 of its 67 counties lost population. Those statements do not conflict: counties have different population sizes, so counting counties does not measure the statewide change.



Percent population change across all 67 Pennsylvania counties. Purple indicates growth; orange indicates decline. Labels identify selected counties discussed below. Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Vintage 2024 estimates and 2024 cartographic boundaries.


The map shows a broad contrast. Many southeastern and south-central counties gained residents, while many western and northern counties lost them. Chester grew by 4.9%, and Cumberland grew by 6.2%. Pike, in the northeast, grew by 6.5%, so the pattern is not a simple east–west split.
Philadelphia lost 1.9% of its population, even as several nearby counties grew. Allegheny also declined, while nearby Butler grew. These contrasts suggest that local planners should look beyond a single city or statewide average. They do not prove that people moved directly from those cities to the growing counties; the data here do not track individual moves between specific places.
I map percentage changes rather than raw counts to compare counties of different sizes. But counts still matter for planning. Pike’s faster growth amounted to 3,831 additional residents, compared with 26,327 in Chester. A high growth rate in a small county can mean fewer additional residents than slower growth in a larger one.

title: A Growing State, but Not Everywhere
text:
What sits behind the change?
Population changes through births, deaths, and migration. The second figure compares seven reference counties from the map. It shows each contribution per 100 residents in the 2020 base, so the values add up to the county’s percentage change. These are cumulative contributions, not annual rates.



Components of population change in seven selected counties. Net migration includes domestic and international migration. The small residual represents the Census Bureau’s remaining accounting adjustment.


Pike and Cumberland gained enough residents through migration to outweigh their excess of deaths over births. Philadelphia shows the opposite balance: births exceeded deaths by 13,896, but net migration reduced its population by 45,280. Allegheny and Erie experienced both more deaths than births and negative net migration. The same outcome—population decline—can therefore involve different balances between these components.

title: A Growing State, but Not Everywhere
section: What the pattern means for planning
text:
What the pattern means for planning
Growing counties may need to examine housing capacity and service demand. Counties losing residents still need to maintain roads and provide services, possibly across a smaller population base. The map helps identify places for closer study; it does not tell officials how much to build or spend. They would also need information about age, housing vacancies, and local budgets.
Several limits matter. County averages hide changes within neighborhoods. Large rural counties occupy more map space without necessarily containing more people. The estimates can change in later releases, and the map’s color boundaries do not mark statistically significant differences. Finally, these data describe population accounting, not why people chose to move. I cannot separate the effects of jobs, housing costs, or remote work from this map alone.
My takeaway is that Pennsylvania’s modest overall growth hides different local needs. The map locates those differences, and the components show why one statewide story is not enough.

title: A Growing State, but Not Everywhere
text:
Sources and reproduction
I download the population estimates and county boundaries directly from the Census Bureau. Its field definitions explain the population components.
My R code joins the files by five-digit county FIPS codes, checks all 67 matches, and maps them with sf in a U.S. Albers equal-area projection. See the README, analysis code, plotting code, county results, or complete reproduction download. The GitHub repository contains the same source files.

title: Education and Unemployment: How Did the Gap Change?
section: 1. All four groups experienced a rise in unemployment
text:
1. All four groups experienced a rise in unemployment



Monthly unemployment rates by education. The shaded interval marks March–June 2020.


The monthly lines show a sharp rise in spring 2020, followed by a decline. Adults without a high school diploma generally have the highest rate, while college graduates generally have the lowest. This shows a persistent difference in unemployment levels. The ranking alone does not tell us whether the gap grew: we need to compare the size of the differences, not just the order of the lines.

title: Education and Unemployment: How Did the Gap Change?
section: 2. Annual rates make the comparison easier
text:
2. Annual rates make the comparison easier



Annual unemployment rates for 2019, 2020, and 2024, calculated from weighted monthly totals.


Among adults without a high school diploma, unemployment rose from 5.5% in 2019 to 11.7% in 2020. For adults with a bachelor’s degree or higher, it rose from 2.1% to 4.7%. All four groups had higher annual rates in 2020 than in 2019, even though their ranking stayed the same.
By 2024, their rates had fallen to 6.3% and 2.3%, respectively. Each group’s 2024 estimate remained above its 2019 value. This is a descriptive comparison, not a claim that these small remaining differences are statistically significant.

title: Education and Unemployment: How Did the Gap Change?
text:
3. Measure the gap directly
For a clear comparison, I define the gap as the unemployment rate for adults without a high school diploma minus the rate for adults with a bachelor’s degree or higher. I measure this difference in percentage points, not percent. This comparison covers two groups; it does not summarize every education gap.



Annual unemployment-rate difference: less than high school minus bachelor’s or higher. Labels show percentage points. Source: weighted IPUMS CPS estimates, ages 25–64.


The estimated gap rose from 3.4 percentage points in 2019 to 7.0 in 2020, then fell to 4.0 by 2024. It did not fall every year: the estimate reached 3.6 points in 2022 before rising slightly in 2023 and 2024. This calculation, rather than the unchanged rankings, supports the description of a larger absolute gap in 2020.
The choice of measure matters. Dividing the two rates instead gives a ratio of 2.67 in 2019 and 2.49 in 2020: the relative gap became smaller. I therefore describe an increase in the percentage-point gap, not an increase under every measure. These are descriptive estimates without confidence intervals. They do not establish statistical significance or show that the pandemic itself caused the change.

title: Education and Unemployment: How Did the Gap Change?
text:
4. Compare adults within age groups



Annual rates within three age groups. Points show only 2019, 2020, and 2024; connecting segments are visual guides. All panels use the same vertical scale and WTFINL weights.


Education groups may contain different mixes of younger and older workers. I also compare rates within ages 25–34, 35–49, and 50–64. The figure shows a similar education pattern within these broad age groups: adults with less education tend to have higher unemployment. This adds detail to the overall comparison, but it does not hold age or other characteristics fully constant. People in the same age band can still differ in experience, occupation, and industry. The figure does not measure the causal effect of a degree.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text: How can we follow a child after they leave their parents’ household? And does an estimate of intergenerational income persistence change when we replace one year’s income with an average across several years? I use PSID data to answer these questions with SQL inside Python. The goal is to show a reproducible match and a careful comparison, not to claim that one estimate captures a causal effect.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
section: Match the people, then their income
text:
Match the people, then their income
Python loads three CSV files into SQLite: people lists personal IDs and birth years, household records the 2000 family relationship, and income records each person’s annual income and age. This part of the full SQL query finds the pairs:
SELECT p.family_id AS origin_family_id,
       p.person_id AS parent_id,
       c.person_id AS child_id
FROM household AS p
JOIN household AS c
  ON p.family_id = c.family_id AND p.year = c.year
WHERE p.year = 2000
  AND p.relationship = 'parent'
  AND c.relationship = 'child';
SELECT chooses the columns we need. JOIN combines two records from the same origin family and year. The relationship conditions make the link explicit. A shared family ID alone would not prove a parent–child relationship in real survey data. After this step, the full query joins each ID to the income table. It uses GROUP BY person_id and conditional AVG to summarize each person’s income within an age window:
SELECT person_id,
       AVG(CASE WHEN age BETWEEN 44 AND 48
                THEN real_income END) AS five_year
FROM income
GROUP BY person_id;
SQLite’s AVG ignores the NULL values produced for other ages. The complete query also counts observations and retains only families with all five years in each window. After loading the CSVs, Python runs that SQL with connection.execute(query) and collects 600 unique matched pairs. The analysis script shows the table creation, CSV imports, and regression calculation.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Calculate the elasticity
I estimate the slope in \(\log(\text{child income}) = \alpha + \beta\log(\text{parent income}) + \varepsilon\). The slope \(\beta\) is the intergenerational income elasticity (IGE). Roughly, a 10% difference in parent income corresponds to a \(10\beta\)% difference in child income in this matched sample. This is an association, not a causal effect.
The data generator gives parents income at ages 44–48 and children income at ages 25–29 and 35–39. All amounts represent simulated, constant-dollar annual personal income. I compare the same 600 families in every row:



Parent measure
Child measure
Estimated IGE




Age 45
Age 25
0.149


Average, ages 44–48
Average, ages 25–29
0.255


Age 45
Age 37
0.311


Average, ages 44–48
Average, ages 35–39
0.418






Four estimated elasticities from the same 600 simulated families. The two early-career estimates are lower than the corresponding midcareer estimates. The simulated long-run sample slope is 0.444.


The generator sets the underlying long-run relationship to 0.45. The realized sample’s long-run slope is 0.444. The one-year estimate at child age 25 sits far below it. The simulation deliberately makes early-career income less closely related to a child’s long-run income. It also adds year-to-year fluctuations to both generations. Thus this exercise builds in the two problems it aims to illustrate; it does not discover their size in real data.
Switching from single-year to five-year measures changes the early estimate from 0.149 to 0.255. That change combines averaging with a shift from child age 25 to ages 25–29, so I cannot credit averaging alone. With the parent measure and five-year length held fixed, moving the child’s window from ages 25–29 to ages 35–39 changes the estimate from 0.255 to 0.418. The simulation’s age pattern drives part of that difference. Averaging helps smooth temporary fluctuations, but it cannot automatically fix a poorly chosen age range. The final estimate comes closest to the sample benchmark.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
What to take away
The SQL match works because we know the relationship at the origin family and follow stable individual IDs after the child moves out. The same matched sample then gives four different IGE estimates when I change the income windows. For a real study, I would need verified parent identifiers, survey weights, checks for missing income, inflation adjustment, and enough follow-up years. This tutorial establishes the matching and measurement logic, not a claim about actual intergenerational mobility.
Run the data generator and analysis script using the steps in the replication guide. The CSV of estimates records the numbers in the figure. The PSID documentation describes the parent-identification data needed for a real application; Haider and Solon explain why annual income can relate differently to long-run income at different ages.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Start with individual IDs
I downloaded two PSID Data Center extracts: the Parent Identification File and a cross-year individual file. The first has 103,725 records; the second has 40,637. In the parent file, PID2 and PID3 identify the child, while PID4 and PID5 identify the birth mother. The individual file uses ER30001 and ER30002 as stable personal IDs. These IDs, not a shared address or household number, establish the parent–child link. The core of the complete SQL query is:
FROM pid AS p
JOIN person AS child
  ON child.id_1968 = p.child_1968
 AND child.person_no = p.child_person
JOIN person AS mother
  ON mother.id_1968 = p.mother_1968
 AND mother.person_no = p.mother_person
SELECT chooses the IDs and income measures we need. JOIN connects the verified mother–child pair to each person’s records. GROUP BY then gathers each person’s income observations, and AVG creates a three-wave measure. For example:
SELECT id_1968, person_no, AVG(real_income) AS parent_avg
FROM income
WHERE income_year IN (2000, 2002, 2004)
GROUP BY id_1968, person_no;
The Python script reads the two fixed-width extracts directly from their ZIP files, loads selected fields into an in-memory SQLite database, runs the SQL, and calculates the slopes. It does not save a person-level matched file.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Compare the same pairs
I use family income, not individual wages. Parent income refers to 2000, 2002, and 2004; adult-child income refers to 2018, 2020, and 2022. I convert each amount to 2022 dollars using annual averages of FRED’s CPI series. The CPI table records the six values used.
The analysis keeps children aged 30–40 in 2023 and birth mothers aged 35–70 in 2005, with a plausible 15–45 year age gap. Each person must have positive, usable income in all three relevant waves and be the family reference person, spouse, or partner in those waves. These rules leave 1,467 mother–child pairs. I use this same selected sample for every comparison.
For each income measure, I estimate the slope in \(\log(\text{child family income})=\alpha+\beta\log(\text{mother family income})+\varepsilon\). Here \(\beta\) is an intergenerational elasticity: a 10% difference in a mother’s family income corresponds approximately to a \(10\beta\)% difference in the adult child’s family income in this sample. It is a descriptive association.








Mother’s family-income measure
Adult child’s family-income measure
Elasticity




2000 only
2018 only
0.303


2000 only
2022 only
0.411


Average, 2000–2004
2018 only
0.373


Average, 2000–2004
2022 only
0.495


Average, 2000–2004
Average, 2018–2022
0.418






Five intergenerational family-income elasticities for the same 1,467 matched PSID mother–child pairs.


With the child’s year fixed at 2018, averaging the mother’s family income changes the estimate from 0.303 to 0.373. With the mother’s measure fixed at 2000, using the child’s 2022 rather than 2018 family income changes it from 0.303 to 0.411. The three-wave average for both generations yields 0.418, which is below the 0.495 estimate that uses only the child’s 2022 income. Averaging does not mechanically raise an elasticity.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
What the comparison can—and cannot—show
One year’s income may reflect a temporary shock or a particular career stage. Averaging several years can smooth short-lived changes, so it may better represent long-run economic status. A separate simulation in this repository makes the life-cycle problem explicit: its designed long-run sample slope is 0.444, while a single early-career year produces 0.149. Those numbers come from invented data, not the PSID.
The real PSID results show sensitivity to timing and averaging, but they do not isolate life-cycle bias. The child’s age changes between 2018 and 2022, and the economy changes too. We also cannot observe each family’s true permanent income. This sample excludes many families without complete positive income records, and I do not apply survey weights. It therefore does not represent a national mobility estimate.
The practical lesson is to verify family links with individual IDs, compare income measures on the same sample, and state exactly what each comparison identifies. The replication guide lists the extract variables, commands, outputs, and privacy rules. It links the aggregate estimates; the raw PSID records remain outside the public repository. Haider and Solon discuss why income measured at different ages can relate differently to long-run income.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
text:
1. Prices and rates moved differently



Real median new-home prices and quarterly-average mortgage rates. Sources: Census/HUD, Freddie Mac, and BLS via FRED.


The median price of a new home rose just 4.5% after adjusting for overall inflation between 2019 Q4 and 2024 Q4. The average 30-year mortgage rate, however, climbed from 3.7% to 6.6%. A home can therefore cost much more each month even when its inflation-adjusted price changes only a little.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
section: 2. Turn those changes into a monthly payment
text:
2. Turn those changes into a monthly payment



Illustrative real monthly payments, with a comparison holding the rate at its 2019 Q4 level. Calculations use 20% down and a 30-year term.


I assume a 20% down payment and a 30-year fixed-rate loan. Under those assumptions, the monthly principal-and-interest payment rose from $1,478 to $2,149 in 2024 Q4 dollars. The dashed line asks what the payment would have been if the rate had stayed at its 2019 Q4 level while prices followed their actual path. At the 2024 price, that payment would have been $1,544, $606 below the modeled payment with the 2024 rate. This gap includes the small interaction between the higher rate and the changed price; it is not the rate-only figure quoted above.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
text:
3. Compare the payment with income



Annualized modeled Q4 new-home payment as a share of same-year U.S. median household income. Sources: Census Table H-5 and FRED series.


This third figure asks a different question: how large is the modeled payment beside a typical household’s income? I multiply each fourth-quarter monthly payment by 12 and divide it by the Census Bureau’s annual U.S. median household income. I use current dollars for both the payment and income in each year. The share rose from 21.0% in 2019 to 31.0% in 2024. Median income grew, but it did not keep up with the payment in this comparison.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
text:
Takeaway
Of the roughly $671 increase in the inflation-adjusted monthly payment, about $580 comes from the higher rate alone and only about $66 from the higher real price alone. Their interaction accounts for the rest. The payment also rose from about 21.0% to 31.0% of median income. For a prospective buyer, the interest rate deserves as much attention as the listing price.
These figures provide a national benchmark, not a measure of what a particular buyer can afford. The new-home median changes with the mix of homes sold; the median-income household need not buy a new home. I also leave out property taxes, insurance, maintenance, fees, and the down payment itself. The price, rate, and CPI data are not seasonally adjusted, so I compare the same quarter in each year. Freddie Mac changed its mortgage survey methodology in 2022.

title: Beyond the Sticker Price: The Cost of Financing a New Home
text:
Data and method
I use new-home prices, mortgage rates, and consumer prices from FRED, plus Census Table H-5 for income. I average the weekly rates and monthly CPI values within each quarter, then convert prices and payments to 2024 Q4 dollars. I calculate the payment for each quarter’s price and rate and repeat the calculation with one 2019 Q4 input held fixed at a time. Those comparisons describe loan arithmetic, not a causal effect of interest-rate policy on house prices.

title: Education and Work: What Unemployment Rates Leave Out
section: 1. Unemployment jumped, but rankings do not show the size of a gap
text:
1. Unemployment jumped, but rankings do not show the size of a gap



Monthly unemployment rates by education. The shaded interval marks March–June 2020.


The spring 2020 spike affected all four education groups. The annual rate for adults without a high school diploma rose from 5.5% in 2019 to 11.7% in 2020. For bachelor’s degree holders, it rose from 2.1% to 4.7%. Their ranking stayed the same, but the difference between those two rates widened from 3.4 to 7.0 percentage points. Dividing the rates tells a different story: the ratio fell from 2.67 to 2.49. The gap grew in absolute terms, not relative terms. By 2024, the difference had narrowed to 4.0 points.

title: Education and Work: What Unemployment Rates Leave Out
section: 2. Count adults with jobs, not only job seekers
text:
2. Count adults with jobs, not only job seekers



Employed share of all adults ages 25–64 by education in 2019, 2020, and 2024. Source: weighted IPUMS CPS estimates.


Unemployment counts only people in the labor force. The next chart instead divides the number with a job by all adults in each education group, including people who are not seeking work. Among adults without a high school diploma, the employed share fell from 58.2% in 2019 to 52.9% in 2020. Among bachelor’s degree holders, it fell from 84.0% to 81.1%. By 2024, those shares were 59.1% and 84.5%. This wider view confirms that a smaller share of both groups had jobs in 2020; the unemployment lines alone cannot tell us that. It also shows a persistent difference in employment levels between education groups.

title: Education and Work: What Unemployment Rates Leave Out
section: 3. Check the pattern within age groups
text:
3. Check the pattern within age groups



Annual rates within three age groups. Points show only 2019, 2020, and 2024; connecting segments are visual guides. All panels use the same vertical scale and WTFINL weights.


The education groups also contain different mixes of younger and older adults. The final figure compares unemployment within three age bands. In 2024, among 25–34-year-olds, the rate was 8.6% without a high school diploma versus 2.9% with a bachelor’s degree or higher. The pattern appears within the older bands too. Differences in age mix therefore do not fully account for the overall education pattern.

title: Education and Work: What Unemployment Rates Leave Out
text:
Takeaway
The 2020 unemployment increase widened the lowest-to-highest education gap in percentage points, even as the ratio between their rates fell. Employment among all adults also dropped in 2020 and had largely recovered by 2024; the education difference remained. The age panels show that this pattern is not just a comparison of young people with older people. Looking at all three views gives a clearer picture of labor-market recovery than a single unemployment ranking.
These are descriptive, WTFINL-weighted estimates for ages 25–64, not evidence that a degree caused the differences. The monthly data are not seasonally adjusted, and the charts do not include confidence intervals. CPS collection changed during the pandemic, which also limits close comparisons.

title: How Much Does County Size Change the Story?
text:
When a county grows quickly, does it also gain a large number of residents? Not always. A small county can grow faster in percentage terms while a larger county adds more people. That distinction matters when local governments think about housing, transportation, and public services.
Living in Philadelphia made me curious about changes across the rest of the state. News about a fast-growing county can sound like a story about a large number of new residents, but the percentage alone does not tell us that. I wanted to see how much the comparison changes when I look at the number of people as well. Pennsylvania offers a useful example because its counties range from small rural communities to large urban areas.
I use Census Bureau estimates for all 67 Pennsylvania counties to compare population change from the April 1, 2020 estimates base to July 1, 2024. This is the same Vintage 2024 dataset I used in Blog 5. Here I use an interactive chart to let readers examine individual counties and compare two ways to measure growth. The Census Bureau has since released newer estimates; I keep the 2024 vintage so the comparison stays consistent with my earlier post.

title: How Much Does County Size Change the Story?
text:
Explore the counties
Each dot represents a county. The horizontal axis shows its 2020 population on a logarithmic scale, so the gap between 10,000 and 100,000 is the same width as the gap between 100,000 and 1 million. Choose a measure to switch between percentage change and the number of people gained or lost. Hover over a dot to see the county name, population at both endpoints, and both measures of change. You can also select a county to highlight it, or click a legend label to show or hide gainers or losers.

  Measure: Percent changeChange in people
  Highlight a county: All counties


The interactive chart requires JavaScript. The linked county data remain available below.

title: How Much Does County Size Change the Story?
section: What changes when we switch measures?
text:
What changes when we switch measures?
Pike County had the fastest percentage growth in the state: its population rose by about 6.5%, or 3,831 people. Chester County grew by a smaller 4.9%, but added 26,327 people. Chester started with about nine times as many residents, so its smaller rate still meant a much larger increase in people. Switching the chart to “Change in people” makes that difference visible.
Montgomery and Cumberland offer another comparison. Cumberland grew by about 6.2%, while Montgomery grew by about 2.7%. Yet Montgomery added 22,777 residents, compared with 16,048 in Cumberland. Montgomery began with more than three times Cumberland’s population. If I ranked counties only by growth rate, I would miss how many more residents Montgomery gained. If I ranked them only by the number gained, I would miss how quickly Cumberland changed relative to its starting size. The two measures answer different questions, and the switch in the chart lets the reader see both for every county.
The chart also shows why the state total can be misleading about local experience. Pennsylvania added about 75,842 residents overall, but 39 counties lost population. Philadelphia lost 29,878 residents, or about 1.9% of its 2020 base. Select Philadelphia to find it among the other counties, then switch measures to compare the size of its loss with the losses elsewhere.

title: How Much Does County Size Change the Story?
text:
Data and reproduction
The data come from the Census Bureau’s Vintage 2024 county population estimates. The starting value is the estimates base, not the unadjusted 2020 census count. The Bureau can revise earlier estimates when it releases a new vintage. I calculate the change as the 2024 estimate minus the base and divide by the base for the percentage change.
The chart uses Plotly’s JavaScript library. The county data, preparation code, chart code, and reproduction instructions are available with the post. The source CSV comes from the checked output of Blog 5; its guide explains how to download and prepare the original Census data.

title: How Much Does County Size Change the Story?
text:
Takeaway
For a county planner, a percentage helps compare the pace of change across places of different sizes. The number of people may matter more when estimating demand for homes or services. Neither number alone tells a planner how many homes to build: household size, vacancies, and population age also matter. The chart describes where changes occurred; it does not show why people moved or trace moves between counties.

title: What Can a Sample Tell Us About a $50 Average?
text:
Suppose a student wants to estimate average weekly spending on groceries. They ask 50 people and find that the sample average is close to $50. How much should they trust that number? A different group of 50 people would probably give a different average. A confidence interval and a hypothesis test give us two ways to describe that uncertainty.
I use a simulated example so we can see the truth that real survey data usually hide. I generate individual spending from a normal distribution with a mean of $50 and a standard deviation of $10. These values are assumptions for a teaching example, not actual grocery data. The charts start with 50 people; use the menu to compare samples of 20 and 100. Each choice shows a separately generated sample and a fresh set of simulations saved with the post.

title: What Can a Sample Tell Us About a $50 Average?
section: 1. Build an interval from one sample
text:
1. Build an interval from one sample
First, I draw one sample from the population. To bootstrap it, I draw the same number of observations from that sample with replacement. Some people can appear more than once in a resample, while others do not appear at all. I calculate the mean each time and repeat this process 500 times. The middle 95% of those bootstrap means, between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, gives a percentile bootstrap interval.


For the sample of 50, the mean is $50.32, and the interval runs from $47.64 to $52.99. The histogram shows how the mean changes when we reuse the observed sample. The interval is not a range containing 95% of individual grocery bills; it describes uncertainty about the population mean.

title: What Can a Sample Tell Us About a $50 Average?
text:
2. Repeat the whole exercise
One interval cannot tell us whether the procedure works in the long run. Here I draw 1,000 independent samples from the population and construct a new bootstrap interval for each one. The chart displays the first 100 intervals. A teal line contains the true mean of $50; an orange line misses it. The count below the chart uses all 1,000 intervals, including those not shown.


With 50 people, 945 of the 1,000 intervals contain $50: 94.5%. That is close to 95%, although it need not equal exactly 95% in a finite simulation. With 20 people, the same run covers $50 in 92.7% of intervals. Simulation noise and the percentile method’s finite-sample accuracy can both contribute to the difference. A 95% confidence level describes the performance of the procedure across repeated samples. Once we compute one interval, it either contains the fixed population mean or it does not; it is not correct to assign that particular fixed interval a 95% probability of containing the fixed mean.

title: What Can a Sample Tell Us About a $50 Average?
text:
3. Test a $50 mean
Now consider a different question: would the observed sample mean be unusual if the population mean really were $50? My null hypothesis is that the mean is $50. For this teaching example, I also assume the population distribution is normal with a known $10 standard deviation. I simulate 5,000 new sample means under those assumptions. The orange tails mark the most extreme 5% of the simulated absolute deviations from $50, split between the two sides.


These charts require JavaScript. The R simulation code and saved results are linked below.



The solid line shows the observed sample mean. I calculate a two-sided p-value as the fraction of null simulations at least as far from $50 as that mean. For 50 people, it is about 0.820, so this example does not reject the null at the 5% level. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It measures how unusual the sample result would be under the stated null model. Both the simulated cutoff and p-value have some Monte Carlo variation; a different random seed can change them slightly.

title: What Can a Sample Tell Us About a $50 Average?
text:
Takeaway
The bootstrap uses one sample to estimate uncertainty, while repeated sampling lets us check how often the interval procedure covers a known truth. A hypothesis test asks a related but different question: how unusual is the observed result under a particular null model? Try changing the sample size and compare the widths and p-values. The sample changes too, so the p-value need not move in one direction. The near-95% coverage here depends on this simulation setup and does not guarantee the same coverage for every population or bootstrap method.

title: What Can a Sample Tell Us About a $50 Average?
text:
Reproduce the simulation
The R script records the random seed, 500 bootstrap resamples per interval, 1,000 coverage samples, and 5,000 null simulations. The chart code, saved results, and README explain how to rerun the example. The Plotly library is included locally, so the interactive charts do not require a live data service.
